title: Acceleration due to gravity using a simple pendulum
description: Find the value of g by timing a simple pendulum at several lengths and using the slope of the l–T² graph.
aim: To determine the acceleration due to gravity (g) at a place using a simple pendulum.
apparatus: Simple pendulum (metal bob with a light, inextensible thread)
Clamp stand with a split cork
Vernier callipers (to measure the diameter of the bob)
theory:
A simple pendulum is a small heavy bob hung from a rigid support by a light, inextensible string. For small angular displacements (less than about 10°) the bob performs simple harmonic motion, and its time period is

\[ T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{l}{g}} \]where \(l\) is the effective length (from the point of suspension to the centre of the bob) and \(g\) is the acceleration due to gravity.

Squaring and rearranging gives

\[ g = 4\pi^2 \frac{l}{T^2} \]

So a graph of \(l\) against \(T^2\) is a straight line through the origin, and \(g = 4\pi^2 \times \text{slope}\). The effective length is \(l = \text{length of thread} + r\), where \(r\) is the radius of the bob.
procedure: Measure the diameter of the bob with vernier callipers at three places and find its mean radius r.
Clamp the thread in the split cork so that the length from the cork to the top of the bob is about 59 cm. Add r to get the effective length l (about 60 cm).
Draw a vertical chalk line behind the mean position of the bob to act as a reference mark.
Displace the bob slightly (less than 10°) and release it so that it swings in a vertical plane without spinning.
Start the stopwatch as the bob crosses the mean position and note the time for 20 complete oscillations. Repeat once more and take the mean.
Find the time period T = (mean time) / 20 and calculate T².
Increase the length in steps of 10 cm and repeat the measurements for at least five lengths.
Plot a graph of l (y-axis) against T² (x-axis), draw the best straight line and find its slope.

calculation:
Mean value of \(l/T^2\):

\[ \frac{l}{T^2} = \frac{0.2481 + 0.2480 + 0.2469 + 0.2487 + 0.2488}{5} = 0.2481\ \text{m s}^{-2} \]

Therefore

\[ g = 4\pi^2 \times 0.2481 = 39.48 \times 0.2481 = 9.79\ \text{m s}^{-2} \]

From the graph, the slope of the l–T² line gives the same value within the accuracy of the readings. Percentage error compared with the standard value 9.81 m s⁻²:

\[ \frac{9.81 - 9.79}{9.81} \times 100\% \approx 0.2\% \]
result: The acceleration due to gravity at the place is found to be g ≈ 9.79 m s⁻² (sample readings).
precautions: The amplitude of oscillation should be small (less than 10°).
The bob should swing in a vertical plane, without spinning or moving in an ellipse.
Start and stop the stopwatch as the bob passes the mean position, where it moves fastest.
The thread should be light and inextensible, and the support rigid.
Measure the effective length to the centre of the bob.
errors: Reaction time in starting and stopping the stopwatch.
Air resistance and friction at the point of suspension.
Error in measuring the effective length.
Large amplitude makes the formula T = 2π√(l/g) inaccurate.

viva.q: Why should the amplitude be small?
viva.a: The formula \(T = 2\pi\sqrt{l/g}\) is derived using \(\sin\theta \approx \theta\), which holds only for small angles.
A pendulum whose time period is exactly 2 s. Its length is about 0.99 m on the Earth's surface.

viva.q: How does the time period change if the bob is made heavier?
viva.a: It does not change. The time period of a simple pendulum is independent of the mass of the bob.

viva.q: Why do we time 20 oscillations instead of one?
viva.a: To reduce the effect of the reaction-time error: the same error is divided over 20 oscillations.

viva.q: What would happen to the time period on the Moon?
viva.a: It increases, because g on the Moon is about one sixth of g on the Earth, so T becomes about √6 ≈ 2.45 times longer.
